extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, and general readers interested in aesthetics and art criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for distinguishing genuine (infectious) art from counterfeit/artifice, and for appraising the merit of art by both formal qualities and subject-matter according to Tolstoy's aesthetic theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infectiousness (contagion) of art
rubrics_metrics.description: There is one indubitable indication distinguishing real art from its counterfeit, namely, the infectiousness of art. If a man, without exercising effort and without altering his standpoint, on reading, hearing, or seeing another man's work, experiences a mental condition which unites him with that man and with other people who also partake of that work of art, then the object evoking that condition is a work of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an internal indication (felt by the receiver) and distinguishes the feeling produced by art from divertisement or mere excitement. The stronger the infection the better the art. Examples/contrast: the authentic infection from peasant singing or a simple child's tale vs. the pseudo-infection from elaborate theatrical spectacle (e.g., Wagner performances) which Tolstoy calls hypnotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of infectiousness as the sole measure of excellence (as art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of the infectiousness of art is the sole measure of excellence in art. 'The stronger the infection the better is the art, as art, speaking now apart from its subject-matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging 'as art' (apart from subject-matter), evaluate how powerfully a work unites receivers with the artist and with one another. Tolstoy states this degree depends on individuality of feeling, clearness of transmission, and the artist's sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality of the feeling transmitted
rubrics_metrics.description: On the greater or lesser individuality of the feeling transmitted: 'The more individual the feeling transmitted the more strongly does it act on the receiver.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work communicates a distinctive, personal state of soul drawn from the depths of the artist's nature. The rarer and more specific the feeling that resonates with the receiver's own unexpressed feelings, the greater the infection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: On the greater or lesser clearness with which the feeling is transmitted: 'The clearness of expression assists infection, because the receiver... is the better satisfied the more clearly the feeling is transmitted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how unambiguously the artist renders the feeling so that receivers can 'mingle souls' with the artist; unclear or unintelligible expression reduces infectiousness even if the underlying feeling is strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity (artist's inner need to express)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the sincerity of the artist, i.e. on the greater or lesser force with which the artist himself feels the emotion he transmits. 'This third condition—sincerity—is the most important of the three... the artist should be impelled by an inner need to express his feeling.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the artist 'writes, sings, or plays for himself' and from inner necessity rather than merely to act on others, gain fame, or please. Insincerity (doing it 'for the receiver') produces resistance in the audience and repels rather than infects. Tolstoy treats sincerity as encompassing and enabling individuality and clearness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of all three conditions required for art; degrees decide merit
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of infectiousness depends on the three conditions (individuality, clearness, sincerity); the absence of any one of these conditions excludes a work from the category of art and relegates it to art's counterfeits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the threefold test together: a work may have varying balances of the three (e.g., individuality+clearness but less sincerity), and these differences decide artistic merit 'as art' regardless of subject-matter. Even a small degree of all three qualifies a piece as art; complete absence of any disqualifies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's subject-matter should promote human progress (evaluated by religious perception)
rubrics_metrics.description: How in art are we to decide what is good and what is bad in subject-matter? Art renders accessible to later generations feelings experienced by predecessors and contemporaries; the more art fulfils the purpose of promoting feelings that move humanity toward perfection, the better it is. The appraisement of feelings is made by the religious perception of the age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging subject-matter, assess whether the feelings transmitted are 'kinder and more needful for the well-being of mankind' and whether they align with the society's religious perception (the era's understanding of the meaning of life). Tolstoy argues that religious perception—explicit or implicit—guides which feelings are beneficial and therefore which subject-matters are 'good.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious perception of the age as the standard for subject-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: In every period there is an understanding of the meaning of life—'the religious perception'—which defines the highest good for that society; art's subject-matter should be appraised by this perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the dominant moral/spiritual direction of a society (Tolstoy's 'religious perception') and evaluate whether the feelings in the artwork make that perception operative in life. Art transmitting feelings contrary to that perception has historically been condemned; art promoting the perception has been encouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counterfeit-art features (borrowing, imitation, effects, interestingness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterfeit art substitutes borrowing, imitating, effects, and interestingness for the infection of feeling: 'It is but a counterfeit of it... manufactured counterfeits of art in which borrowing, imitating, effects, and interestingness replace the contagion of feeling.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag works that prioritize poetic kitsch, historical or archaeological imitation, spectacular effects, novelty of sounds/technique, cleverness, and manufactured 'interest' over genuine transmission of feeling. Examples: elaborate Wagnerian spectacle, imitative stagecraft, technical innovations that 'interest' rather than infect. Such features may produce divertisement or hypnotic assent but are not art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulative presentation and spectacle as signs of counterfeit (hypnotism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle and presentation designed to hypnotize or manipulate (e.g., darkness, concealed orchestra, prolonged exposure) can produce an apparent unanimity of delight but are not evidence of art: 'That success I explain... he produced a model work of counterfeit art... thanks to his exceptional position... he was able to command all the methods for counterfeiting art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of institutionalized or sensory manipulations that manufacture audience assent (Bayreuth example). These conditions (repetition, enforced environment, social signaling) can cause collective enchantment without genuine infection; they are an anti-pattern when used to mask lack of sincerity/individuality/clearness.

rubrics_metrics.name: External ornamentation, technical 'perfection', and novelty do not guarantee art
rubrics_metrics.description: In our society the external quality of the work in false productions is not only no worse, but often better, than in real ones; the counterfeit is often more effective than the real, and its subject more interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate polished technique, ornate presentation, or novelty of modulation/effects with true artistic value. Evaluate whether such externals serve the transmission of feeling (infection) or merely fascinate and pervert taste. Tolstoy warns that connoisseurs and critics can be misled by externals into praising counterfeits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's purpose: making feelings accessible across generations
rubrics_metrics.description: Art, like speech, is a means of communication and therefore of progress; speech renders knowledge, art renders feelings—'art renders accessible to men of the latest generations all the feelings experienced by their predecessors...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising an artwork consider whether it successfully communicates and preserves feelings so that later generations can share them; works that fail to transmit persistent, socially relevant feelings fall short of art's historic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity demonstrated by simple, direct works (folk/peasant examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy uses examples of peasant singing, a simple child's story, and folk-music as genuine art because they 'transmit a definite and strong feeling' and result from sincerity and collective feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use folk/peasant/naïve works as exemplars: if a work transmits feeling simply and directly (no artifice), it is likely authentic. Contrast with celebrated 'high' works that are technically complex but fail to infect (e.g., certain later Beethoven works, ornate academic paintings).
